activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them.
story:
At the canoe dock on Thursday morning, the whole morning at camp seemed to revolve around one thing: the penalty shot game Mr. Bakker had set up on the sandy court. Leah lined up behind Grady and Sylvie, each of them waiting for a turn to kick the ball through the gap between two orange cones. She had missed twice already, and her socks were filling with sand, which she felt was a separate unfairness but not one worth arguing about.

Sylvie kicked next, and the ball rolled wide of the cones. "That was close," Sylvie said. "I think close ones should count half a point." Grady spun around so fast his water bottle flew off the bench. "You only want that because you just missed! If you'd kicked it through, you'd never say it." Sylvie crossed her arms and looked obstinate, chin up, mouth set, like a seagull guarding a french fry. The line behind them went quiet, and Leah felt the game slipping away before anyone had even scored.

"Wait," Leah said. She walked over and stood between the cones, thinking. "Sylvie's rule isn't a bad rule. It's just a bad time for it." Grady frowned. "What's the difference?" Leah picked up the ball and held it. "If we'd all agreed on the half-point rule before we started, it would have been fair, because nobody would know yet whether it would help them or hurt them. Deciding it in the middle, right after your miss, means you already know. That's the difference." Sylvie chewed her lip, then nodded slowly. "So we could still use it." "Sure," Leah said. "For the next game. We write it in the rules before anyone kicks."

Grady found a stick and scratched the rules into the wet sand near the dock: half a point for a cone-rattler, full point through the gap, everyone gets five kicks. He even added, at the bottom, RULES ARE FOR BEFORE, in letters so large they looked like the title of a very short, very sandy memoir. On the next round, Sylvie's kick rattled the cone and earned her half a point, and Grady's kick went wide, and neither of them complained once. Leah went last. Her sock was still full of sand, but the ball sailed straight through the gap, and she raised both arms and shouted, "Full point!"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
story:
The train had been rolling for an hour when Theodore unfolded his new book, and within twenty minutes the carriage began to swim around him. His stomach rolled with it. He pressed his palms against the seat and stared at the steady grey ceiling, waiting for the queasiness to pass, but every sway of the carriage brought it back.

Across the aisle, his neighbour Ms. Paquette watched him close the book and swallow hard. "Going to visit your grandmother?" she asked, because they had boarded together at the same small station and she knew his family's plans. Theodore nodded, then carefully opened the book again. The words blurred. His stomach lurched. He shut it and groaned.

Beside him, Augustin leaned over from the window seat. "You look green. Do you want to swap places? We caused a whole controversy over who got the window when we got on, your sister and me, but you can have it now." Theodore slid over gratefully and put his forehead near the cool glass. Outside, rain had saturated the fields until they shone like ponds, and fence posts streaked past in long ribbons. He watched a farm gate rush by, then a church, then a whole village, and bit by bit the queasiness drained away.

He turned it over in his head. Reading in a car on a winding road had done this to him before, every single time, yet sitting still made it stop. Why? He stared at the book on his lap, then at the rushing landscape, and an idea formed. When he read, his eyes told his brain one thing, that he was still, because the page never moved. But the balance organs in his inner ear felt the sway and rattle of the carriage and told his brain the opposite, that his body was moving. The two signals conflicted, and the clash made him sick. When he looked out the window instead, his eyes saw the world streaming past, which matched what his inner ear felt, and the signals agreed.

He decided to test it. "Augustin, time me," he said, and picked up the book. For a minute he read, and the rolling feeling crept back. Then he looked out the window at the saturated fields flashing by, and it faded again. He tried it twice more, watching the horizon each time his stomach warned him, and each time the trick worked.

Ms. Paquette smiled at the two of them passing the book back and forth. "You've figured out motion sickness all by yourself," she said. Theodore balanced the book on his knee, eyes fixed on the racing horizon, and read aloud the first sentence to Augustin.

activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
knowledge_domain: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
fact: A piece of furniture turned at a different angle from the walls gets its own pair of vanishing points, but they still sit on the same horizon line.
story:
Laurence sat on the back step with her sketchbook, her pencil hovering over a half-finished drawing of a living room. Mr. Chukwu, the neighbour who watered his tomatoes every afternoon, had shown her two-point perspective last weekend, and she had practised walls and windows until her fingers ached. Today she wanted the room to have furniture, and that was where the trouble started.

She drew the armchair angled toward the television, then tried to run its lines to the same vanishing points she had used for the walls. She wince and erased it, then wince again, because the chair looked like it was melting sideways. Her mother joked that good drawing was hereditary on her grandfather's side, but Laurence knew that was nonsense. Her grandfather drew horses with five legs. This wasn't about blood. Something was wrong with her idea.

Harley dropped through the gap in the fence and leaned over her shoulder. "The chair's doing something weird," Harley said. "Did you break the room?"

"The room's fine," Laurence said, though she remembered a moment last week when she had ignored Mr. Chukwu's advice about rulers and freehanded a whole street, then thrown it away. Maybe this was the same thing: rushing instead of thinking. She stared at the chair, then at the walls, then at the horizon line that ran across the whole page. She had assumed the chair had to obey the same points. But what if it didn't?

She set a fresh pair of vanishing points for the chair, careful to keep both of them sitting on that one horizon line, and drew the armchair again. This time it sat solidly in the room, turned toward the television, as if someone had just left it.

"Whoa," Harley said. "It's got its own secret points?"

"On the same horizon line," Laurence said. "Every angle gets its own."

Mr. Chukwu, listening over the fence, smiled at his tomatoes.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
story:
The school called it at six in the morning, and by six thirty Brooklyn was dressed and out the back door with two sleds, a shovel, and a Thermos of cocoa. Bryn arrived next, dragging Elyas by the sleeve of his coat. They had never seen the backyard like this. The fence was a soft white line, and the picnic table had turned into a single rounded shape, like a loaf of bread.

They started building a fort against the fence, packing snow block by block. Brooklyn dug the doorway low so the wind couldn't whip straight in, and after a while the three of them sat inside on their sleds. Elyas pulled off one glove and flexed his fingers. "It's warmer in here," he said. "That can't be right. It's all snow."

Brooklyn had brought the kitchen thermometer in her pocket, because she liked to check things. She read it outside the doorway, then held it inside for a full minute. The numbers were higher inside, by quite a bit. She turned the snow block in her hand and looked at it closely. It was full of tiny holes, like a sponge. "It's mostly trapped air," she said. "Fresh snow, I mean. All these little bubbles. So it works as an insulator, like a blanket." Bryn frowned. "Snow can't be a blanket." "A cold blanket," Brooklyn said. "It keeps the cold out and the warm in, instead of the other way around."

"Then how do the rabbits do it?" Elyas asked. Brooklyn traced a line in the snow with her mitten, then another that branched off it, until she had drawn a whole network of tunnels under the crust. "Like this," she said. "Mice and shrews stay under there all winter. It's zero degrees at the surface and warmer down in the tunnels, and the wind can't reach them at all." Bryn still looked doubtful, so Brooklyn had an idea. She packed a hollow in the fort wall and set the thermometer inside it, sealed with loose snow. "Ten minutes," she said.

They waited, drinking cocoa, and when Brooklyn pulled the thermometer out, the reading had climbed again. Bryn leaned over her shoulder to see it and then sat back on her sled. "Okay," Bryn said. "I believe the rabbits." Elyas poked his head out the doorway. A mouse had crossed the yard, leaving a stitch of tracks, and vanished into a small hole near the shed. "It's got a whole authentic snow house under there," he said. Brooklyn packed another block onto the wall.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Jonathan tapped his phone and watched the group chat scroll. Twenty-three messages since lunch, all because someone had posted a screenshot of Romie's photo, the one of her dog wearing the unicorn costume she had made herself. The screenshot came from an account called dylan_447, and Jonathan was almost sure he had seen that name before, back when Romie's account was public and she accepted anyone who asked.

"But my account is private," Romie typed. "I checked. It says private."

Jonathan pulled up her profile. The little lock was right there. He remembered, though, that dylan_447 had followed her months ago, before the lock, and had never unfollowed. He typed slowly, testing the idea as he wrote. "Private means people who don't follow you can't see it. But dylan already followed you. So he still could." He added, "Anyone you already accepted can still copy or share what they see. Even a screenshot."

Romie's reply came as three dots, then a long pause, then a voice message. "Wait. I only accepted him because he said he liked my dog videos. I don't even know him." Her voice wobbled at the end.

Jonathan scrolled back through dylan_447's account, being systematic about it, checking each post one by one. Two other screenshots of Romie's photos. One of Cristiano's skateboard trick, captioned with a laughing emoji. Jonathan sent Cristiano a private message: "This guy is reposting our stuff. Screenshot it before he deletes it." Cristiano answered with a thumbs up and then wrote, "My mom always said don't accept people you don't know. I thought it didn't matter. Guess I was wrong." That was new. Cristiano usually argued about everything.

They met at the picnic table behind the library after school. Romie brought her dog, no costume this time, and the dog tried to mimic Jonathan when he stretched his arms wide, standing up on its back legs as if it wanted wings. Romie laughed for the first time all day. "Okay," she said, holding her phone out. "You three are the only ones I'm keeping. Everyone else, gone." She tapped through her follower list, removing dylan_447 first. Cristiano leaned over her shoulder. "Do mine too. And I'm turning off location, since it was tagging the skate park every time I posted."

Jonathan watched dylan_447 disappear from the list. Then he opened his own follower count and started counting how many of them he actually knew. "Hey Romie," he said. "Can you help me check mine?"

She scooted over on the bench and patted the wood beside her. "Start from the top," she said. "One at a time."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers, and the animals that eat them are called secondary consumers.
story:
Mila slid her notebook across the lab table and tapped the empty box at the top of her page. "Sun," she announced, and drew a big rayed circle. Mr. Levy had said the whole class had to build a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator by the end of the period, and whoever explained it best got to feed the axolotls. Mila wanted that job more than anything.

"So after the sun, grass," said Lohan, leaning over from the next station. "Then what? My chain keeps getting too short."

"That's because you're skipping a whole level," Mila said. She remembered the farm trip last fall, sorting animals with her cousin. "Remember at the farm? The goats and rabbits ate the plants. My cousin called them primary consumers. Animals that eat only producers, that's what they are."

Hendrix spun his chair around, pencil already out. "Then the animals that eat them, the fox and the hawk, those are secondary consumers. My chain goes sun, grass, rabbit, fox, hawk." He said it fast, like a race announcer, and Mila laughed and copied it down.

"But here's the part I actually want to figure out," Mila said, standing up so fast her stool squeaked against the floor. "What if one link disappears?" She grabbed the eraser and hovered it over the word grass. "Hypothesis. If I erase the grass, the rabbits have nothing to eat." She wiped the word out and drew a thin arrow of crumbs from grass to rabbit, then a big red X. "No grass, no rabbits. And then?"

"No foxes," Hendrix said slowly, watching the chain. "The hawk might eat more rabbits first, but if the rabbits are gone, everything above them wobbles."

"The whole top of the chain is vulnerable," Lohan said, and Mila pointed at him like he'd scored a goal. She drew it out: the producer gone, the primary consumers shrinking, the secondary consumers with nothing to hunt. Then she added the hawk's line up to a jagged peak at the top and labeled it "climax," because that's where the chain ended, at the top predator nobody else dared eat.

When Mr. Levy walked by, Mila flipped her page toward him. "We tested it with an eraser," she said. "Remove one link, the levels above it collapse." He looked at the drawing, then at the axolotl tank, and held out the container of bloodworms. Mila took it with both hands, grinning so hard her cheeks hurt, and sprinkled the worms into the water. The axolotls lunged.

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: Finely grated cheese melts faster and more evenly into a sauce than chunks of cheese do.
story:
Jaxon had already dumped two failed pots down the drain, and the community kitchen's Saturday class was only halfway through. Mr. Hu had shown everyone how to melt butter, stir in flour, and whisk until the mixture turned smooth, a base called a roux. Jaxon's roux came out fine. It was the cheese that kept betraying him. The first time, the sauce had clumped into rubbery islands that refused to cooperate no matter how hard he whisked. The second time, he'd gotten frustrated and cranked the heat, which only made things worse.

"Third pot," he announced, setting it on the burner. "I'm like a defendant getting one more chance from the judge."

"Judges don't usually give third chances," said Brennan, who was measuring milk at the next station.

"Then I'm lucky Mr. Hu isn't a judge." Jaxon melted the butter, added the flour, and whisked until the roux smelled nutty and looked glossy. So far, so good. He poured in warm milk a little at a time, and the sauce thickened into something silky. This was the exact moment where everything had fallen apart before.

Across the table, Oceanne was struggling with her own pot. She had cut her cheddar into big cubes and dropped them all in at once, and now she stood waiting while they bobbed in the sauce, stubborn and solid. "Why won't they just melt?" she groaned.

Jaxon watched her cubes drift around, and something clicked. His first two attempts had used chunky cheese too, and the sauce had lumped while he waited. Maybe the chunks were the whole problem. "Oceanne, how big are those pieces?"

She held one up. It was the size of a dice.

At the cheese station there was a box grater, and Jaxon remembered that his grandmother grated cheese into tiny fluffy piles for her macaroni. He grabbed the grater and a fresh block. "Try this." He grated until a soft mountain of fine shreds covered the board, and Oceanne ladled them into her pot a handful at a time.

Within moments the shreds vanished into the sauce, melting fast and smooth, no lumps anywhere. Brennan leaned over and peered into her pot, then into Jaxon's. "Yours still has chunks, dude."

Jaxon didn't argue. He dumped his chunky cheese, grated a fresh pile, and stirred it in slowly. The sauce turned glossy and even, better than anything he'd made all morning. Mr. Hu walked past, glanced into the pot, and gave him a thumbs up.

"Taste it," Oceanne said, holding out a spoon.

Jaxon blew on it, tasted, and grinned. "One more batch. I want to get it perfect before lunch."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Grandma's kitchen smelled like honey cake, which was torture, because Isabelle had decided she was going to try the Yom Kippur fast this year. Not the whole thing. She was twelve, and her parents said she could do part of it, like her cousin had done at her age. But she wanted to get it right, and right was where the problem started.

"How long does it actually last?" she asked, following Grandma to the window where the sun was sinking behind Mr. Li's fence. "Twenty-four hours? Sunset to sunset?"

Grandma just smiled and lit the holiday candles, which Isabelle took to mean figure it out yourself. That was fine. Isabelle loved figuring things out. She sat at the table with a piece of paper and built a little algorithm in her head: if the fast starts at sunset tonight, and the holiday ends when three stars are visible tomorrow night, then sunset tomorrow isn't the finish line. Nightfall comes after sunset. She ran the steps forward, sunset plus sunset plus extra dark sky, and her pencil stopped. It wasn't twenty-four hours. It was about twenty-five, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.

"Twenty-five hours!" she announced, so loud that Mr. Li looked up from watering his roses across the fence.

"You'd better advocate for a bigger breakfast tomorrow," Grandma said, setting out the last meal before the fast began, "because twenty-five hours is a long time to go on one plate."

Isabelle ate like it was her job. Her friend Denzel had texted her a countdown app idea, but she told him no app could beat watching the sky. She kept her goal objective and simple: no food, no drink, until the stars came out tomorrow, and Grandma would point at them and say the blessing, and then there would be soup.

Morning came, and her stomach growled like a small angry animal. She drank nothing. She thought about the honey cake in the tin and walked to the window instead, counting clouds. The afternoon crawled. By the time the sun touched Mr. Li's fence again, she felt hollow and oddly light, like a balloon with the string cut.

"Almost," Grandma said beside her.

"Not almost," Isabelle said. "After nightfall. That's the rule."

So they waited in the darkening yard, and when Isabelle spotted the third star, she jumped up and pointed at it, shouting toward the fence, "Mr. Li! Look! That one's mine!"

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Isabelle had exactly fifteen minutes before the nurse would call her name and her one chance would be gone. She had spent the whole drive rehearsing the question, and now she kept losing the first word of it.

Katelynn sat beside her, swinging her sneakers against the chair leg. "My sister got hers in fourth grade," Katelynn said. "Ten years old. My mom made pancakes about it, which was weird."

"Leah's sister didn't get hers until she was almost fourteen," Isabelle said. "Leah told me yesterday. Fourteen." She turned the corner of a magazine page back and forth until it creased. "That's a giant difference. Ten to fourteen."

"So?" said Katelynn.

So everything, Isabelle thought. Half the girls in their grade already had theirs, and Isabelle was eleven and a half and still waiting, and she could not figure out whether that meant she was behind, or normal, or what. The pattern didn't make sense to her. If Katelynn's sister was ten and Leah's sister was fourteen, then there couldn't be one single schedule everyone followed. There had to be a rule underneath it, something she was missing.

When the nurse finally called her, Isabelle blurted it out before the blood pressure cuff even came out. The nurse didn't laugh. She said Dr. Ruiz would answer that one herself, and she handed Isabelle a thin pamphlet from the rack by the sink. On the back page, in small print, Isabelle found it: a big CDC survey had found the median age of a girl's first period in the United States was about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it. She read the line twice. Median meant the middle, the halfway point, so half the girls were earlier and half were later. Ten and fourteen both fit inside a wide range. It wasn't a race with a deadline after all.

Dr. Ruiz came in, asked her usual questions, and said, "Still sleeping well? No late-night, nocturnal screen use?" Isabelle admitted to reading under the covers sometimes. The doctor checked a box marked sleep, one small category on the form among others for growth and eating, and said, "Everything looks right on schedule. Your own schedule."

On the drive to school, Isabelle texted Katelynn from the back seat: the middle is about 12, and a wide range is normal, so we're both fine. Katelynn sent back a pancake emoji and the words "fourteen is allowed too."

Isabelle looked out the window at the pharmacy sign going by and slid the pamphlet into her backpack, next to her library book, where she could find it again.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Violet laced her sneakers in the community center gym, where the smell of floor wax and popcorn mixed in the hot air. Her volleyball team, the Comets, had lost every away game this season. Every single one. But last Saturday they had won at home, and then again on Tuesday, and Violet had begun to suspect something.

She remembered the first away game, back in September. The bus had rattled for forty minutes, the other gym had felt huge and echoing, and the Comets had played like strangers. "Why do we look like a different team out there?" she had asked Teresa on the ride home, and Teresa had only shrugged.

Now Violet spread her notebook on the bleachers. She had written down every result, home and away, for all the teams in the league, plus the scores her cousin had texted her from the soccer league and the basketball league. A pattern jumped out. At home, teams won more than they lost, over and over, in sport after sport. Not just the Comets. Everybody.

"Fiona, look at this," she said, tapping the columns. "Every league, not just ours. Home teams win more than half their games, on average. All of them."

Fiona squinted at the notebook. "My brother says that's called home advantage."

"Home advantage," Violet repeated, testing the words. She had one more idea to test before the coach blew the whistle. "Then we should play like it. Be aggressive right from the first serve, since we're on our own floor."

When the whistle finally blew, Violet called the first set high and hit it clean. Fiona dug a ball that seemed impossible to salvage, scooping it off the hardwood and popping it up into the light. The crowd stomped the bleachers until the whole gym thundered.

The Comets won their third straight home game. In the hallway afterward, Teresa grabbed Violet's arm. "Next week's away. Think your notebook travels?"

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: In call-and-response singing, a leader sings a line and the group answers; the pattern is deeply rooted in African musical traditions and in gospel and work songs.
story:
Ellie practiced at Fairview Cemetery because her great-grandmother was buried there, under the cedar with the cracked stone, and because nobody else came on Tuesday afternoons. The song she was learning had come down through four generations of her family, and Ellie was supposed to sing it at the Juneteenth gathering in two weeks. The problem was the structure. Somebody sang a line first, and everybody else answered after, but Ellie kept starting her answer too early or too late, so the whole thing collapsed.

"Try watching my mouth instead of listening," said Jannat, who had come along with Killian to help. They stood between the rows of stones while Ellie faced the cedar. Jannat sang the opening line, slow and clear, and Killian waited until she closed her mouth on the last word before he came in with the answer. Ellie watched, and for the first time she caught the seam between the two parts. It wasn't a pause exactly. The leader finished, and the group's answer landed right behind it, like an echo that chose its moment.

"It's called call-and-response," Killian said. "My grandpa says it came out of African musical traditions, and it runs all through gospel and work songs. He learned it picking tobacco, singing across the rows." That gave Ellie an idea. If the pattern worked across a field, it might work across a cemetery too. She made Killian stand thirty feet off, behind a tall monument, where she couldn't see him at all. She sang the call. His answer floated back over the stones a half beat later, and it still fit, because the rule didn't depend on seeing. It depended on the leader finishing first.

Mr. Foster, who tended the plots along the north fence, stopped raking to listen. He told them the gathering would be small this year, since the recession had emptied out half the town's donations box, so every voice would matter. Then he asked who was leading the call at the event. Jannat and Killian both looked at Ellie. Her mother had been supposed to lead it, but her mother worked Saturdays now, ever since the layoffs. Ellie took a breath, faced the cedar, and sang the first line out across the quiet rows of stones.

Jannat's voice came in behind her, right on the seam.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Collecting money on Free Parking in Monopoly is a common house rule, not one of the official rules, which is why players from different homes argue about it.
story:
The rain hammered the craft cabin so hard that Mr. Suzuki gave up on kayaking theory and let the campers dig through the games shelf. Eli pulled out a Monopoly box with a wobbly lid, and Ishaan yelled dibs on the racecar before anyone else could grab it.

Everything went fine until Ishaan landed on Free Parking and rubbed his hands together. "Pay up," he said, pointing to the middle of the board, where Elsie had been stacking the unused bills in a neat pile. "That's the pot. Taxes and everything go there, and whoever lands on Free Parking takes it."

Elsie frowned. "We don't do that at my house. Free Parking is just a rest stop. Nothing happens."

Ishaan leaned back with his arms crossed. "Everybody plays it my way. That's the rule."

Eli watched the two of them and wondered if the problem was really about the money. Maybe it was about whose house the rules came from. That would explain something he'd noticed: Ishaan and Elsie weren't cheating, they just believed different things. He held up a hand. "Wait. Before we fight, let's name the problem. The problem isn't Free Parking. The problem is we never agreed on what Free Parking means."

Ishaan squinted. "Meaning it means money."

"Meaning we don't know," Eli said. He lifted the wobbly lid and reached underneath the board to retrieve the little rulebook, folded and soft at the corners. He flipped through it while the others crowded in. There it was, printed in small type: landing on Free Parking did nothing. No pot, no payout. But Ishaan's version wasn't made up either, because Eli's own family played it that way at home, collecting the taxes in the middle and handing the pile to whoever landed there. It was a house rule, something families added themselves, which had to be why players from different homes argued about it.

"So both of us were right," Ishaan said slowly, "and both of us were wrong."

Eli grinned. "So here's my idea. We agree on one rule right now, before anything else happens. We could play the official way, or we could all vote on the house rule. Either way, it's our rule, not somebody's mom's rule."

They voted. The house rule won, two to one, and Ishaan retrieved the stack of bills from Elsie's pile and planted it in the center of the board like a flag.

"Better land on it soon," he said. "My bankruptcy is imminent."

"Then you should charge your tenants more," Elsie said, tapping his half-empty row of properties. "Read your title deed card."

Eli rolled the dice and moved his thimble, watching the board with new eyes, wondering what other arguments were hiding inside other games.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and rubber, and forty girls were already warming up when Kayla laced her sneakers. Tryouts for the school team started in ten minutes. She was bouncing a ball to Kennedy when Coach blew the whistle and called, "Forms on the table before you step on the court! Signed forms only!"

Kennie's face went pale. "What forms?"

"Physical forms," said Jolene, jogging past. "The doctor ones. You can't try out without a signed checkup form. School rule."

Kayla remembered then, quick as a snap of fingers: two weeks ago, her mom had taken her to the clinic, and a clinician there had listened to her heart, checked her eyes, and signed a paper. Mom had said, "Put this in your backpack tonight, not later." Kayla had a flashback to herself stuffing it in the front pocket while her mom watched, arms crossed, until the zipper was all the way closed.

She unzipped the pocket. The paper was still there, folded once, still signed. Relief poured through her like cold water.

But Kennedy stood frozen by the bleachers. "I never went to a doctor. Nobody told me."

Kayla thought about it. Coach hadn't asked who was tall or fast. The very first thing she'd asked for was the form, before anyone touched a ball. So that was the rule that came first, before anything else. Maybe there was a way around it, and maybe there wasn't, but standing here guessing wouldn't help. "Come on," Kayla said, pulling her friend toward Coach.

"Coach, Kennedy didn't know about the physical. Can she watch today and bring the form tomorrow?"

Coach studied Kennedy for a long second. "She can sit on the bench and learn the drills. Then no practice until a doctor signs her form. Deal?"

"Deal," Kennedy said, grinning.

Later, while they ran suicides, Kayla's lungs burned, and she cherished every burning breath, because tryouts were hers to fight for now. Jolene passed her the ball with a distinct snap of the wrists, and Kayla let it fly.

"Swish!" Jolene shouted.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: On a shaded sphere, the highlight is the brightest spot, on the side facing the light, and its position shows where the light is coming from.
story:
Owen stared at the circle he had drawn in his sketchbook, then at the orange sitting on the kitchen table beside it. Mr. Nowak had told the art club to practice spheres over the weekend, and Owen wanted his to look round instead of flat. His circle was gray all over, like a gray fungus had grown on the page, and no matter how he squinted at it, it refused to become a ball.

Juan came over after lunch, carrying his own sketchbook, and flopped into the chair across the table. He leaned over Owen's drawing and frowned. "Which side is the lamp on?"

"What lamp?"

"In your picture," Juan said. "There has to be a lamp somewhere, right? Otherwise nothing would be lit."

Owen looked at the desk lamp at the end of the table, its light spilling sideways across the orange. He picked up the orange and held it in the beam, turning it slowly. On the skin, one small patch caught the light and gleamed brighter than everything else, brighter even than the parts that were merely pale. He turned the orange a little more and the gleam slid across the peel, always staying on the side that faced the lamp.

"Okay," Owen said slowly. "So there's a bright spot, and it's on the side toward the light." He set the orange down, grabbed a fresh sheet, and drew a new circle. This time he left one small patch almost white, high on the left side, right where the lamp's beam would hit. Then he shaded harder and harder as he moved right, until the far edge of the sphere was nearly black. Under the ball, he smudged a dark oval leaning away from the lamp.

"That's better," Juan said. "Can you elaborate on the shadow under it? Make it darker near the ball."

Owen pressed harder with his pencil, firm and assertive, until the cast shadow looked like it was really sitting on the table. He held the drawing up next to the orange and compared them. In his picture, the bright patch sat on the left, exactly where the real one did, and the whole sphere suddenly pushed out from the page like something he could pick up.

"Now try one with the light coming from the other side," Juan said, reaching over to spin the lamp around.

Owen flipped to a clean page and started a new circle.

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: In traditional and competition Irish step dancing, dancers keep the upper body and arms held still while the feet do fast, intricate footwork.
story:
Aiden had signed up for Irish step dancing at the community hall mostly because Devyn dared him to, and he had been biased against it from the start, expecting something slow and boring. He was wrong about that within the first ten minutes. The music was quick, the stomps rang off the wooden floor, and his feet were expected to move faster than he thought feet could move. "Watch me demonstrate the reel," said Ms. Chea, and then she did something that made no sense to him at all. Her feet hammered out complicated rhythms while her whole upper body stayed perfectly still, arms at her sides, as if the two halves of her belonged to different people. That was the rule, he realized as he watched: the upper body and arms stay still while the feet do the fast, intricate footwork.

He tried it and failed immediately. His arms flapped like he was swatting mosquitoes, and every time his feet sped up, his arms sped up too. Adnan, who had been taking classes since September, laughed but not in a mean way. "Everyone does that at first," he said. "My arms were worse than yours."

Aiden couldn't stop thinking about it on the walk home. His arms weren't trying to ruin things on purpose, so why did they move? That night he remembered something from the summer, a flashback that flicked on like a light: he was learning to ride his bike with no hands, and every time he wobbled, he gripped the handlebars harder without deciding to. His body had just done it. Maybe his arms were the same. Maybe they weren't flapping because he was bad at dancing. Maybe they flapped because his balance was wobbling and his arms were catching him, and he couldn't see that happening.

The next class, he tested his idea. He asked Ms. Chea if he could press his hands flat against his sides while he practiced, and she said that was exactly what beginners did. With his hands pinned there, his arms couldn't flap, and he noticed something: he stopped tipping forward so much. When he deliberately slowed his steps for one run-through, his arms stayed quiet all by themselves. The flapping hadn't been the problem. The flapping had been the symptom.

He told Devyn and Adnan after class, both of them out of breath, all three sitting on the stage edge while the seniors' tea dance group set up tables in the hall for their pension club meeting. "My arms were like a wobbling bike," Aiden said. "Fix the wobble, fix the arms."

"Okay, genius," Devyn said, "then demonstrate."

Aiden hopped up, pressed his hands to his sides, and hammered out the first eight steps, still as a post from the waist up.

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: 'Very' plus a weak adjective can usually be swapped for one stronger word, such as 'exhausted' for 'very tired' or 'freezing' for 'very cold'.
story:
Florence's story was due at the end of library period, fifteen minutes from now, and every line had the word "very" in it. Tatum leaned over from the next seat and pointed at the page. "You wrote 'very tired' twice in one paragraph."

Florence read her draft again. The hero was very cold, very scared, and very hungry, and the tower was very tall and very dark. "It sounds flat," she said, "but if I cut the very's, it just sounds tired. Cold. Hungry. Still flat." She tried crossing out one and it didn't help. Her pencil hovered, and she felt like the whole page was her adversary, winning.

Then she noticed something. Ms. Farah-Ali had left a chart on the shelf by the window, and Jaxson was reading it. "Listen to this," he said. "'Very tired' can just be 'exhausted.' And 'very cold' is 'freezing.'" Florence grabbed her pencil. Her hero wasn't very cold, he was freezing. The tower wasn't very dark, it was pitch-black. One stronger word where two weak ones had been, every single time. She worked down the page, testing each line, and the sentences stood up straighter.

Now the words were better, but the rhythm was still wrong, every sentence the same length, chug chug chug. "Restrict yourself," Tatum suggested. "Make the next one really short." Florence wrote: "He ran." Then a long sentence after it, then another short one. She read it aloud under her breath and the paragraph moved like she wanted it to, quick and then slow. When the bell was two minutes away she carried the page to Ms. Farah-Ali's desk and set it down. "It's better," she said, trying not to sound too proud, but feeling buoyant anyway, like her draft was floating. Ms. Farah-Ali read the first line out loud: "The exhausted climber stared up at the freezing peak."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, the Governor General, or a deputy such as a Supreme Court justice, gives royal assent to federal bills on behalf of the monarch.
story:
On election day, Ms. Castillo marched Lea's whole class through the gymnasium door of the polling station with clipboards and one stern instruction: talk to voters, learn something, and do not touch the ballot boxes, which looked mysterious and slightly sinister behind their cardboard screens, like voting happened inside a fort. Lea's clipboard had a real problem on it. Her civics assignment was due tomorrow, and she still could not explain how a bill became a law. She could explain how toast became burnt toast, but that was not on the assignment.

"The trick is finding a voter who knows," Isla whispered, eyeing the line of people in camouflage jackets, running shoes, and one enormous knitted hat shaped like a beaver.

Lea had a plan. She would test every voter with the same question and see who answered without making a face like she had asked them to spell "legislature" backwards. "Excuse me," she said to the first person, "how does a bill become a law?"

"Slowly," the man said, and shuffled on.

"That's data," Leopold said, writing it down with great seriousness. "One vote for slowly."

The second voter said "committee something," which was closer, and the third asked Lea to hold her coffee. Then Lea spotted a woman in a long black robe standing near the voter services table, looking like she had wandered in from a courtroom on her way somewhere important.

"Excuse me," Lea said. "You look like a judge."

"I am a judge," the woman said. "I'm here to participate in the election like everyone else. You can't wear the robe to vote, apparently, but here we are."

"Then you must know how a bill becomes a law!" Lea held up her clipboard like a shield.

The judge raised an eyebrow. "Parliament passes the bill, and then royal assent is given by the Governor General."

Lea scribbled it down, then squinted at the robe, the judge, the robe again. A thought crept up on her, quiet as a rumor. "Wait. Can someone else do it? If the Governor General is, like, on vacation?"

The judge smiled, clearly enjoying this. "A deputy can give royal assent instead. Someone such as a Supreme Court justice."

"A judge! You! You could approve a whole law?" Lea imagined it: robes, a gavel, a law being born. "Could you do it right now? Just, boom, law?"

"I could, in the right circumstances," the judge said, "but today I'm mostly approving of that beaver hat."

Lea wrote everything down in giant letters, thanked her about four times, and dragged Isla and Leopold over to repeat the whole thing as practice. "Parliament passes it," she recited, "then royal assent, Governor General, or a deputy, such as a Supreme Court justice."

"Slowly," Leopold muttered.

"Fine," Lea said. "Bill becomes a law, slowly, unless a judge is standing around in a robe." She flipped her clipboard shut with a snap.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
story:
Emmett stood at the counter in the mall eyewear shop, turning his new glasses over in his hands. The frames were plain and cheap, because his mother had been frugal since the recession had cost her cousin a job, and she said glasses would be broken or lost within a year no matter what they cost. Emmett couldn't argue with that. He had lost two water bottles and one shoe already this year. He put the glasses on, and the room snapped into focus so sharply that he grabbed the counter. Behind him, Eve waved, and he could actually see her face, not just a pink blur with teeth.

Ms. Jung, the optician, checked the fit behind his ears. "Astigmatism," she said, tapping his lens. "Your lenses are cylindrical, so they bend light more in one direction than in the other." Emmett nodded, but he didn't really follow, and he was too busy staring at a sale sign across the mall to ask.

While his mother paid, Eve pulled him toward the fountain. He took the glasses off to clean a smudge, and that was when he noticed it. Holding one lens up, he looked through it at the fountain and the whole scene looked stretched, like taffy. He tipped the lens sideways, ninety degrees, and now the water looked squashed instead of stretched, tall and skinny. He tried it again. Through one way, wide. Through the other way, narrow. Same lens, same fountain, different world.

"So the lens bends light more in one direction," he said slowly, turning it again to justify the conclusion before he said it out loud. "That means the stretching has to follow the lens, not my eyes. If I rotate it, the stretching rotates too." He spun the glasses in a slow circle and watched the fountain lean, widen, lean back, like something breathing. Eve leaned in next to him, one eye shut, and grabbed the other lens. "Mine does it too," she said. "Trade."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
Aspen's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn, and Tyler sat at the counter with her phone glowing between them, staring at a comment on Jet's post. Jet had written "first day of track practice, wish me luck," and underneath it, from a kid named Derek in their grade, was one line: "you run like a broken vacuum, quit now." Tyler read it twice. Derek held doors for people. Derek said "excuse me" in the halls even when nobody was in his way. Tyler could not make the comment and the boy fit into the same person.

"That doesn't even sound like him," Aspen said, chewing a nail. "He lent me a pencil yesterday. Sharpened." She scrolled down, and there was another one, worse, the kind of thing Derek would never say out loud in the cafeteria where everyone could see his face.

Tyler remembered last fall, when he had typed something snotty to a kid in another town after a game, something he'd deleted two days later, feeling sick. Sitting alone with his phone at home, in his room, with the door shut, it had been easy to hit send. He wondered if that was it, if the screen itself changed people, and whether saying it in public would eliminate the meanness the way sunlight killed germs. He decided to test it. He typed a reply to Derek: "say that to Jet at school tomorrow, in front of everyone, same words." Then he put the phone down and drank his juice, watching the translucent baggie of orange peel on the counter like it was a specimen.

At school the next morning, Tyler hung back by the water fountain while Jet passed Derek in the crowded hall. Derek looked at Jet, opened his mouth, and then studied his shoes until Jet was gone. Jet came over with a half-smile. "So he's not going to say it, huh."

Ms. Charles passed them carrying a stack of folders and paused. "You two look like you caught something."

"More like an infection that only lives in phones," Tyler said. "It's called the online disinhibition effect. This psychologist, John Suler, wrote about it in 2004. People say stuff online they'd never say to your face."

Ms. Charles raised an eyebrow and moved on, and Jet turned his phone over in his hand, thumb hovering. "So do we tell him, or just watch him tomorrow?"

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
story:
The morning of the tryouts was cold enough that Luke kept his jacket on while he laced his cleats, though he knew the thin insulation would not matter once he started running. He stood at the edge of the field with Hashim and Theoren, all three of them watching the older players practice on the far side. Twenty-six boys were trying out for sixteen spots on the school team, and Luke had been pessimistic about his chances all week.

"I'm not warming up," Theoren said. "I don't want to waste my legs before Coach even looks at us."

"You sure?" Luke asked.

"I want to watch the eighth graders first. See how good they are." Theoren leaned against the fence and folded his arms inside his sleeves.

Hashim had already started an easy jog along the sideline. Luke hesitated, then followed him. They ran a slow lap, then another, and after that they did moving stretches, walking lunges and leg swings and high knees, nothing hard. Luke felt his breath come quicker, and by the end his legs were warm under his shorts even though the air still bit at his face.

Hashim grinned at him. "Light jogging and moving stretches raise your heart rate and your muscle temperature. That's what makes your muscles ready for a hard effort."

Theoren snorted from the fence, where he had been standing still for fifteen minutes, watching the eighth graders take shots.

When the whistle blew, the coach had them sprint the length of the field. Luke flew down the grass, legs light and quick. Beside him, Theoren took three fast strides, then his hamstring seized and he stumbled, grabbing the back of his thigh. He limped to the sideline, jaw tight, and sat down on the cold ground.

The tryout went on. Luke integrated himself into a small-side scrimmage, calling for passes, dropping back when the ball swung to his wing. He could hear Theoren calling from the sideline, "You're doing fine, keep going," and Luke lifted a hand to show he'd heard.

At the end, the coach read the numbers from a clipboard. Luke's number was seventh on the list. He stood still for a second, then found Theoren still sitting in the damp grass.

"I'm sorry," Luke said. "You were faster than me in gym."

Theoren rubbed his leg and looked at the field. "Next tryout," he said, "I'm running the laps with you two. And you're carrying my jacket, since yours keeps you so warm."

Hashim tossed him the jacket. "Deal. Now come on, we'll jog you back slow."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, a la derecha means to the right, but derecho, as in sigue derecho, means keep going straight, and learners often confuse the two.
story:
Sebastian's grandfather had one rule for the summer: no English before noon. Abuela enforced it from her kitchen, where she was teaching Sebastian to bake pan dulce, and the sweet smell of cinnamon drifted out to the patio where he sat with his flashcards.

"Abuela," he asked in slow Spanish, "¿dónde está la panadería de Karl?" Karl lived two streets over, and he had promised to meet Sebastian at the little bakery near the plaza, but Sebastian had never walked there alone.

Abuela wiped flour from her hands. "Desde la plaza, sigue derecho hasta el mercado, y después a la derecha." Sebastian nodded, repeated it, and set off. At the plaza, he thought about her words. Derecho, derecha. The two contradicted each other in his head, or seemed to, and he made a choice: he turned right immediately, onto a narrow street of shuttered houses.

The street curled away from the market. A dog followed him for a block, then lost interest. When the road dead-ended at a wall of bougainvillea, Sebastian sat on the curb and considered his mistake. He replayed Abuela's sentence. She had said two different words, and only one could mean "right," because the second one had come after, as if it were an extra instruction. So derecho, the word inside sigue derecho, must mean something else. He tested the idea by reversing his turn: back to the plaza, then straight, past the church, until the market rose up ahead, and then, at last, one turn to the right.

Karl was leaning against the bakery counter, arms crossed, half a sweet bread already eaten. "You're late," he said in English, which Sebastian decided to allow, since noon had come and gone. "I was going to leave. I wanted to get the good ones before Brock's cousin buys them all, and I was about to give up on you."

"Sigue derecho means keep going straight," Sebastian said, mostly to himself, "but a la derecha means to the right. I turned right when she told me to go straight on." He felt his ears go warm, remembering the curb and the dog.

Karl grinned and slid a paper bag across the counter. "So what you're saying is, your Spanish needs a critique."

"It needs practice," Sebastian said, and broke off a piece of the bread, which was still warm, the most sophisticated thing he had eaten all summer. Outside, church bells rang the hour, and he pointed down the street toward home. "¿Sigo derecho?" he asked Karl.

"Una cuadra más," Karl said, "y después a la derecha."

Sebastian walked on, straight past the corner, waiting for the right one.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
story:
Quinn had never seen her grandmother skip a meal before. Grandma was the kind of person who measured rice like it was treasure and checked the warranty on her ancient rice cooker twice a year, "just in case." So when Quinn arrived at her grandparents' house on Saturday and Grandma served a huge breakfast at ten o'clock, then ate nothing at noon, Quinn started paying attention.

"Are you sick?" she asked, setting a plate of noodles in front of her grandmother.

Grandma laughed and pushed the plate back. "I'm fine. Today is uposatha," she said simply. "I took eight precepts this morning, and one of them is not eating after midday."

Quinn sat down across from her. She knew her grandmother was Buddhist, and she knew about the little shrine in the hallway with its parallel rows of candles, but she had never heard the word uposatha before. Eight precepts sounded like a lot of rules. Not eating after midday sounded, honestly, impossible. Quinn got cranky if she had to wait even an hour past lunchtime.

She wondered if Grandma was secretly hungry and just being polite. Maybe Grandma had simply forgotten, or maybe she'd be glad if someone reminded her. So Quinn tried an experiment. She peeled a mandarin, set the slices on a saucer right next to Grandma's teacup where the smell would be strongest, and watched from the doorway. Grandma looked at the mandarin. She looked at Quinn hiding badly behind the doorframe. Then she smiled and folded her hands in her lap, and the mandarin sat there untouched while she went back to her chanting.

That was when Quinn understood it wasn't forgetting. It was choosing. Grandma had known exactly what the orange was doing there, and she still didn't take a single slice. When Quinn came back in and ate the mandarin herself, Grandma didn't scold her either. "The precepts are mine for today," she said. "You eat when you're hungry, child."

That gave Quinn an idea. If she couldn't eat after midday on uposatha days, she'd have to allocate her food to the morning instead, the way Grandma had with that giant breakfast. So the next time uposatha came around, Quinn asked to try it too. She ate a big bowl of rice and vegetables at eleven, and at three in the afternoon, when her stomach growled during Grandma's chanting, she drank water and counted the candle flames instead.

"How long until sunset?" she whispered.

Grandna checked the window, where the light was just beginning to turn gold. "About an hour," she said. "The kitchen opens then."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
Aiden stared at the group chat, thumb hovering. Dante had sent a photo of a poster from the community centre wall with the message "someone drew a vase with a face on it, weird." Yani replied three seconds later: "That's not a vase, it's two faces looking at each other." Aiden zoomed in. He could see the vase, plain as a glass on his kitchen table, but the more he looked, the more the white in the middle seemed to shift, like the moment rain precipitation on a window refract was impossible, so he typed instead: "It's a vase. Yani, zoom in."

"It's two faces," Yani sent, with a screenshot of the same poster cropped tighter. "Aiden, the outline is two noses." Dante sent a row of question marks, then "you're both looking at the same poster and seeing totally different stuff?" That was the part that bothered Aiden. Same picture, same wall, same afternoon light. One of them had to be wrong, and he wanted it settled before dinner.

Ms. Bianchi, who ran the centre's art room, had her number on the notice board, and Aiden had messaged her once about a lost jacket. He sent her the photo now and asked whose version was right. Her reply came while he was watching rain streak the kitchen window, droplets refracting the porch light into little wobbly stars. "Neither and both," she wrote. "That's a Rubin vase, from Edgar Rubin, a Danish psychologist, in 1915. You can see it as a vase or as two faces, but not both at the same moment."

Aiden read it twice, then looked at the photo again. The vase held steady for a second, then his eyes caught the faces and the vase vanished completely. He typed, "Yani's right," then deleted it, because that wasn't quite true either. Dante was already messaging: "so who won?" Aiden pasted what Ms. Bianchi had written and added, "nobody, that's the whole point." Then he set the phone face down, picked it up again, and sent one more line: "meet me at the centre tomorrow, we'll stare at it until it flips."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: An oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius.
story:
The recipe had come from an American website, and Carter read it three times before he touched anything. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees, it said, then mix the dry and wet ingredients separately. His mother's oven, the old one with the sticky door, only showed Celsius. He had promised his friend Charlotte he would bring blueberry muffins to her bake sale table on Saturday, and Charlotte had already texted him twice that morning.

"I'm counting on you," her message said. "I want our table to beat Carina's. She's bringing those lemon bars everybody likes, so my whole plan depends on your muffins. You can do this. You're more meticulous than anyone I know." Carter put the phone down and stared at the dial. He had let the recipe intimidate him all week, but he wasn't going to let a number beat him now.

He turned the dial to 350 and watched the little light blink on. Then he paused. If the recipe was American, he thought, then the 350 was probably Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit degrees were smaller than Celsius ones. That meant 350 of them should be fewer than 350 of the ones on his oven. But how many fewer? He took out his phone and searched, and there it was: an oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit was about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. He clicked the oven off, turned the dial back down to 175, and clicked it on again, feeling like he had just cracked a code nobody in the kitchen could see.

While the oven heated, he measured the flour carefully, cracked two eggs, and folded in the blueberries without crushing them. His mother wandered past and asked if he needed help. "I've got it," he said, spooning batter into the paper cups. "Almost." He slid the tray in, set the timer for twenty minutes, and stood in front of the glass door watching the muffins rise like a small ecosystem of their own, each cup leaning into its neighbor.

They came out golden, domed, and slightly blue at the edges. Charlotte texted him a photo of the empty table with one line: "Saturday, 9 a.m., bring all of them." Carter wrapped the muffins in a tea towel, wrote "350 F = about 175 to 180 C" on a sticky note, and pressed it to the fridge for next time.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at each pole.
story:
Arianna spread the map across the kitchen table and weighed the corners with salt shakers. Anabelle leaned over it, holding a list of cities her mom had printed for their family trip: Quito, Cairo, Mexico City, Nairobi.

"I get to pick one extra stop," Anabelle said, "but Mom says I have to prove it's near the equator. She says I need to stop guessing." She tapped the paper with her pen. "My tutor said the answer is on the map, but he wouldn't tell me how to find it."

"Then we'll figure it out ourselves." Arianna traced her finger across a line near the middle of the map. A tiny label read 0 degrees. "This must be it. It says zero right there, and the equator crosses Africa and South America."

"So what do the other lines mean?"

Arianna followed a curved line upward from the equator toward the top of the map, where the numbers climbed to 90. Then she traced downward and found another 90 at the bottom. "Latitude," she said, reading the small word in the legend. "It says latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator. Zero at the equator, and ninety degrees at each pole."

"So a smaller number means closer to the equator?" Anabelle grabbed the pen. "Quito is almost on the zero line. Cairo's way up at thirty." She circled Quito so hard the pen tore a little hole in the paper. "Quito! Mom can't argue with degrees."

"See if you can find Mexico City and Nairobi too," Arianna said. "You'll need more than one piece of evidence."

Anabelle frowned at the map, which seemed determined to be obstinate, folding itself at the crease whenever she let go. Arianna dropped two more salt shakers on it, and the paper finally lay flat.

Anabelle measured Nairobi with her thumb, circled it, and jumped up. "Mom! I have proof!" Her footsteps propelled her down the hallway, the list flapping behind her like a flag.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
story:
Elena had left her water bottle on the kitchen counter, and by the time she noticed, her mother's car was already pulling into the rec centre lot. The pool here had almost closed last spring until the landlord agreed to fix the leaking pipes, and now the whole neighbourhood thrived on summer swim sessions. Today, though, the lot was packed with kids from school, all trying out for the swim team, and the sky had that volatile grey look that kept flipping between sun and cloud.

"Third heat is the long one," said Connie, knotting her cap. "Four hundred metres. Mr. Perera makes everyone swim it last."

"That's my heat," Elena said. She felt fine during warm-up, fine during the sprint heats too. But halfway through the four hundred, her arms turned heavy, as though someone had poured wet sand into them. Her kick, which had been crisp in the first heat, went sloppy and slow. Heaven touched the wall a full length ahead of her, and Elena dragged herself out at the ladder, dizzy and strange.

She stood dripping by the bleachers, trying to work it out. She had not been slow in the sprints, so it was not her fitness. The difference was the long heat at the end of a hot afternoon, and she had drunk nothing since breakfast. She remembered a poster in the change room about hydration, something she had skimmed and forgotten. On the way past it she stopped and read properly: losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events. She looked at her own hands, still pruned, and thought, that was me. Two percent. She weighed herself on the lobby scale before and after her soak at the fountain, and the numbers told the same story.

Mr. Perera posted the list at the end of the day. Elena's name was near the bottom, in the last qualifying spot, with a note beside it: last heat times looked off, re-swim Monday. She found Connie by the door. "Monday I'm bringing two bottles," Elena said. "One for before, one for between heats." Connie grinned and bumped her shoulder, and outside the clouds finally split into real rain.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Pumice is an igneous rock full of gas bubbles trapped as lava cooled, and many pieces are light enough to float on water.
story:
Ryan crouched at the tide line with three buckets labelled IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY and METAMORPHOUS, which Ria immediately crossed out and rewrote as METAMORPHIC. "Mr. Pelletier will do a rock census," she announced, tapping her clipboard. "Every rock on this beach gets counted and sorted by how it formed. Igneous from cooled lava, sedimentary from squished layers, metamorphic from heat and pressure." Gregoire held up a gray lump. "And if we get it wrong?" "Then the census is wrong forever," Ria said gravely, as if a government agency depended on them.

Ryan picked up a pale, holey stone that looked like a gray sponge. He dropped it into the sedimentary bucket, because holes made him think of sand. Then he frowned. He knew sedimentary rocks formed from layers, but this stone had no layers at all. He took it out, turned it over, and made a decision scientists everywhere would respect: he threw it into a tide pool to see what happened.

It bobbed. The rock floated, spinning slowly like a tiny gray raft. "Rocks don't float," Gregoire said, staring. "That one does," Ryan said. He fished it out and held it up. "Igneous bucket. It's full of gas bubbles trapped when lava cooled. That's why it's so light." Ria consulted her clipboard. "It's called pumice." Gregoire sniffed. "Saying a rock floats feels subjective." "It either floats or it doesn't," Ryan said, and dropped it back in. It floated again, smugly.

That evening Ryan's grandfather found a message taped to the fridge: "Dear Grandpa, beach census complete. 41 rocks sorted, 3 arguments, 1 floating rock named Admiral Bob. Pumice is igneous, full of gas bubbles from cooling lava, and light enough to float. Come see him do laps in the sink." His grandfather found Admiral Bob in the kitchen bucket and lowered him into a bowl of water. "Well," he said, giving the rock a gentle push, "sail on, little captain."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42, right after dinner. Kim had posted first: "Did anyone SEE what happened in the hallway today? The two kids who collided outside the gym?" Jeremy had seen it, sort of, from the water fountain. He remembered books flying and someone yelling, but when he tried to pin down details, they kept sliding around. Anya replied, "Yeah I was right there. It was bad." That was the trouble. "Bad" could mean anything.

Jeremy wanted the truth because Mr. Sadeghi had announced that anyone who saw the collision should write a statement for the office, and he resented having to rely on other people's memories instead of his own. So he tried something. He messaged Kim privately: "How fast was the first kid going when he smashed into the other one?" She answered, "Fast. Like running really hard, maybe a sprint." Then he messaged Anya the identical question, word for word except one: "How fast was the first kid going when he hit the other one?" Anya wrote back, "Not that fast honestly, kind of a jog, he tried to stop."

He sat staring at the two replies. Same hallway, same moment, two descriptions that were nowhere near equivalent. He scrolled up through the chat and noticed the pattern held: people who used dramatic words described the collision as violent, and people who used plain words made it sound small. It reminded him of a page Mr. Sadeghi had shown the class once, about a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, where people asked how fast cars "smashed" into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that "hit." He had thought it was boring then. Now he tested it on himself, asking his own memory both ways, and got two different collisions.

"Wait," he typed to Kim. "Try asking your brother the hit version and see what he says." Three minutes later she sent back a screenshot. Her brother had estimated a slower speed, same as Anya. Jeremy read it twice, then opened his statement for the office and deleted his first sentence, which began "The kid came out of nowhere, flying." He wrote instead, "I was at the water fountain and heard a crash. I saw books on the floor." Then he added one last line to the chat: "Everyone send me your answers exactly as you gave them, and include the question I asked you." Kim replied with a single eye emoji.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
John slid a folded paper under his plate before his dad could see it. Across the table, his little sister was telling a long story about a bee, and John used the noise to study the numbers he had copied during recess: every time he touched the ball in Saturday's game, and what happened after.

"John, you're moving your lips," his dad said. "What's under the plate?"

He handed it over, because there was no way out. "It's my touches. Elie counted them for me. Eleven touches, and six times the ball went to somebody on our team after me."

His dad looked at the paper for a while, and then he laughed, which was not what John expected. "You know what this reminds me of? Moneyball."

"Money ball?"

"It's a book," his dad said. "Came out in 2003. Michael Lewis wrote it. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." He tapped the paper. "A low-budget team, using numbers to compete with rich teams. Everybody else was ranking players the old way, and Oakland was looking at different numbers."

John chewed on that along with his rice. So one number, like a ranking, could squash eleven touches into a single word, good or bad. But what if the single number was the wrong one? He tried to imagine what his coach saw when he looked at him. Probably the two goals John gave away. Nobody had counted the passes that kept the ball moving.

"Can I speculate about something?" he asked, and his dad raised an eyebrow the way he did when John used a word from his vocabulary list. "The coach ranks us by goals. But Parker got six goals and lost the ball like twenty times. Nobody wrote that down."

"Maybe the coach doesn't have a Parker column," his dad said.

"Maybe that's the whole problem," John said. "There's no column for it."

At school the next day, John showed Elie the paper and proposed a truce: no arguing about who was better, just one week of counting everything, both of them, even the boring stuff. Elie agreed, then ruined the truce immediately by arguing that blocked shots should count double, and they spent all of lunch negotiating. By Friday the chart had grown so long it looked like a corroding pipe in science class, spotted and eaten away at the edges, but the numbers held.

On Saturday, John taped the chart inside his binder and carried it to the bench where the coach sat. He waited for halftime, took a breath, and held it out.

"Coach," he said. "I found something Parker does that nobody's counting."

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: With three strides between hurdles, a hurdler takes off from the same foot every time, because an odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading.
story:
Sadie counted under her breath as she ran toward the first hurdle: one, two, three, jump. The little plastic bar wobbled but stayed up, and she landed, sprinted, counted again, and clipped the second hurdle hard enough to knock it flat into the grass.

"Same foot?" Victoria called from the bleachers, where she was supposed to be resting her twisted ankle but was instead keeping tally on a napkin.

"Wrong foot every single time," Sadie said, walking back to the start. The coach had set the hurdles close together in the far corner of the park, and the morning sun refracted off the dew so the whole row glinted like a string of aquariums. "I count three steps, but I always take off from my left, and my right is my lead leg. I jump crooked."

Tess jogged over, breathing hard from her own turn. "You hit four, then three, then three," she said, squinting at the napkin Victoria waved at her. "You're not consistent."

Sadie stood at the start line and did the math out loud, because thinking while running had not worked so far. "Three steps between hurdles," she said slowly. "Left, right, left. Then I take off from my left again. If I take off from my left at the first one, three steps means I take off from my left at every one after that, too. An odd number of steps keeps the same leg leading." She looked up. "So it's not random. I'm not arriving on the wrong foot by accident. If my first takeoff is wrong, they'll all be wrong."

"Then fix the first one," Victoria said. "Lead with your left at hurdle one, even if it feels weird."

It did feel weird, like writing with the wrong hand, and Sadie's first attempt was a graceless hop that made Tess laugh until she had to sit down on the grass. But the bar stayed up. She walked back, shaking out her arms, and tried again. Left lead, three steps, left lead again, three steps, left lead. The fourth hurdle, the one she had flattened twice, passed beneath her so cleanly she barely felt it leave the ground.

Afterward, sprawled in the shade near the duck pond, Tess pointed at a green film on the water. "That whole slick is one organism, my science teacher says. Algae, all connected." Sadie watched a dragonfly land on it, its wings intricate as lace, and thought that the hurdles were connected too, each one deciding the next.

Victoria limped over with a water bottle and held it out without being asked. "You stopped counting out loud on the last run," she said.

Sadie took a long drink and grinned. "Left, right, left. I don't have to count anymore. I just hear it."

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
