fact: Many credit cards charge no interest on new purchases if the full statement balance is paid by the due date; this is called a grace period.
story:
Jonathan stacked the last crate of honey jars and checked his phone. Four weeks of Saturdays at Mr. Martínez's farm stand meant fifty-two dollars in his pocket, and the skateboard he wanted cost one hundred forty.

"You keep counting that money like it's going to hatch," Jaya said, laughing. She worked the cash box on Sundays and was saving for concert tickets, which was all she talked about.

"It's too slow," Jonathan said. "The shop might sell out of the board. My dad said I could put it on his credit card and pay him back later." He paused. "But he said there'd be interest. Like a fee for borrowing."

"Then it costs more than the sticker says," Jaya said. She frowned, then brightened. "Wait. My mom uses her card every single week, groceries and everything, and she never pays interest. I've seen the statements. Zero."

"That's bizarre," Jonathan said. "Borrowing money for free?"

Jaya shrugged. "She said it's called a grace period. She pays the whole bill by the due date, every time." Jonathan inhaled the smell of warm apples and thought so hard he almost dropped the crate. Interest on the card was like an infection, small at first but spreading if you let it grow. If Dad paid only part of the bill, the interest would start. But if the full statement balance got paid by the due date, there was no interest on the new purchases at all.

"I'm going to test it," he announced. "Small. Dad puts the board on the card, I hand him twenty-six dollars every Saturday, and we pay the whole thing off by the due date. If a fee shows up, I was wrong."

Mr. Martínez, who had been listening while weighing tomatoes, gave him the next Saturday off to visit the shop. Jonathan raced home to ask.

"Dad," he called through the screen door, waving his envelope of cash. "I've got a plan."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
story:
Arthur had fasted from breakfast until sundown, the way his family did on certain holy days, and now he stood at the front of the community hall with his stomach growling and a plan in his head. His little sister had been promised she could hold the Havdalah candle tonight for the first time, and Arthur had promised Tyson and Cataleya they could come watch. The problem was that they kept asking questions he could not answer by pointing at anything yet, because the tables at the front were still bare.

"So what actually happens at this thing?" Tyson asked, sitting on a folding chair with his sneakers swinging.

"You'll see it in order," Arthur said. "That's how I figured it out myself. First there's a cup of grape juice, then spices you smell, then the candle. I used to think the candle was just decoration, but that turned out to be an illusion. Watch the wicks."

When his sister lifted the candle, Cataleya leaned forward. "It's braided," she said. "And there's, like, more than one wick in it."

"Several wicks," Arthur's sister said, holding it out flat on her palms the way she had practiced in the kitchen all week. "Ms. Pelletier told me to keep it level so the wax doesn't drip on the cloth."

Ms. Pelletier, who ran the hall, dimmed the overhead lights. The cup of grape juice went up first, then the spice box passed from hand to hand. Tyson took a sniff and held it a second longer than everyone else. "Cloves," he whispered to Cataleya, and she whispered back, "I think there's cinnamon too." Arthur noticed that Tyson lingered on the smell while Cataleya shrugged after one breath, which made him think that liking a smell had to be subjective, the same way his sister loved cloves and he only tolerated them.

After the blessings, the flame was dipped into the cup and went out with a small hiss. A thread of smoke rose, twisting, and Arthur waved his hand to pull the scent toward him, the way his father always did. "The smoke dissolves before you can really follow it," he said. "That part you can't hold onto."

"Can I try?" Tyson asked, and stood up.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The ancient Egyptian pyramids were built as tombs for pharaohs, meant to protect the king's body and belongings for his life after death.
story:
Arianna spread her worksheet on the flat base of the war memorial, where the carved names caught the afternoon light. Lennox sat on the step beside her, chewing his pen.

"The pyramids were palaces," Lennox said. "Giant houses for the kings. Obviously."

Arianna looked at the model photograph on the sheet, the one from the museum. A palace had windows, halls, kitchens, a place for a hundred people to eat. The pyramid in the picture had one narrow passage leading to a small room with a stone box in it. She turned the paper so Lennox could see. "Would you build your palace with no windows and one room? Where's the throne?" Lennox leaned closer and frowned. She tapped the little room. "That's a burial chamber. The whole thing is a tomb, built to protect the pharaoh's body and his belongings for his life after death." Lennox said his uncle had once told him an anecdote about a king buried with his dogs, which proved nothing, but he wrote "tomb" in the blank anyway.

The second question was harder: why did their farms depend on the Nile? Arianna thought about what she could not see from the picture, the reason underneath. She picked up a stick and drew in the gravel beside the memorial: a river, a line of floodwater spreading over the fields. Every year the river rose, covered the land, and when the water pulled back it left dark mud. She scattered a few pebbles like seeds on the mud. "Seeds germinate in that wet soil," she said. "No river, no mud, no crops." Simeon, who had been copying names off the memorial wall for a project, wandered over. "So the flood was good news? That's backwards." Arianna drew a dry gully next to the flooded field. "Flood, then food. No flood, then that."

Simeon studied the two drawings, then the carved names above them, people the town had built stone to remember. "The Egyptians built stone for their dead too," he said slowly. Arianna nodded and started writing her answer in the last blank.

A barn owl, nocturnal and hunting early in the dusk, swept over the memorial and out toward the river.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Sweat and bacteria stay in worn clothes and socks, so changing into clean ones each day helps prevent body odor.
story:
The gym was loud with squeaking shoes, and Mr. Banerjee blew his whistle for the third time. Naomi grabbed the rebound and passed to Dereck, who scored, and for a second everything was good. Then Mckayla leaned over during the water break and whispered, "Naomi, no offense, but something smells like a locker room that lost a fight."

Naomi sniffed her sleeve and her stomach dropped. She had put on deodorant that morning, the same kind her mom bought, and she had showered last night. So why did she still smell? She could not stop thinking about it all through math, drawing little arrows in her notebook. If she was clean and wearing deodorant, the smell had to come from somewhere she had not checked. What was left? She looked down at her hoodie, the gray one she wore basically every day because it was not flammable like her cozy fake-fur one, which her dad said was basically a fire hazard near the stove.

After school she found Mckayla at the lockers. "Can I test something on you?" Naomi asked. "It's a science experiment, kind of."

"You're weird, but okay," Mckayla said.

"Hold this." Naomi handed over the hoodie and stood a few feet back in just her T-shirt. Mckayla sniffed the hoodie, gagged dramatically, then sniffed the air near Naomi's shoulders and raised her eyebrows. "Okay, that's the factor right there. You smell fine. Your hoodie smells like a sock that's been through a war."

"So it's the clothes," Naomi said slowly, working it out aloud. "The sweat gets in them, and it just stays there, and it doesn't matter if I'm clean underneath." She thought of the poster Mr. Banerjee had pointed at during health class last week, the one meant to illustrate good hygiene habits, with a little drawing of a shirt in a laundry basket. She had stared right at it and missed the whole point.

That night she pulled the gray hoodie out of the hamper and stuffed it in the washing machine, along with every shirt, sock, and pair of shorts she had worn that week. The next morning she came downstairs in a clean hoodie, fresh socks, and deodorant, and her mom said, "Look at you. What's the occasion?"

"Hygiene," Naomi said.

At morning practice, Mr. Banerjee split them into teams, and Mckayla jogged over to Naomi's side. "I'm guarding you," she said, grinning. "You smell like laundry now. Toughest defense I'll face all day."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
Jaxson set his fork down and stared at his grandmother. She had just finished telling the whole table, for the second time, about the ginger tea from Ms. Boateng that cured her monster headache on Tuesday. "Worst one in months," she said, tapping the teapot like it was a treasure. "By Wednesday morning, gone." Jaxson wanted to believe her. But something nagged at him, the same feeling he got when a magic trick seemed too perfect. His dad always said bad headaches come and go. What if Tuesday's headache was going to leave anyway?

He decided to test it. That night he made a chart in his notebook and asked his grandmother to rate her headache every evening from one to ten. She laughed and agreed. Tuesday, the tea day, was a nine. He kept the chart going, even when it got tedious, filling in little boxes while she watched her shows. Kingston came over for dinner on Friday and studied the numbers. "So the tea only got tried on the really bad one," Kingston said slowly. "She never drinks it on a two." Jaxson grinned. That was exactly the hole in the story.

He found the name for it on Saturday, in a library book about how people fool themselves. He ran to Ms. Boateng's porch to speculate about it out loud. "The book called it regression to the mean," he said. "Unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones. So if you try a remedy when symptoms are at their worst, you might improve even if it does nothing." Ms. Boateng nodded. "My mother swore by honey water for the very same reason, I'd guess."

At Sunday dinner, Jaxson laid the notebook beside the mashed potatoes. "Grandma, the tea might work, or the nines might just turn into threes on their own. To know, you'd have to drink it on the mild days too, or skip it on the bad ones and see." His grandmother looked at the chart for a long moment, then at the teapot. "Well then," she said, pouring herself a cup, "we'd better start skipping some Tuesdays."

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Interest is the price of borrowing money, usually charged as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
story:
Juliette spread the Skyrider VR headset box across the cafeteria table like evidence in a trial. Two hundred forty dollars, said the sticker, though the sticker was polite about it and called that a sale price.

"You could just save up," said Thalia, poking the box. "You have ninety in your jar."

"By the time I save the rest, everyone at school will have moved on to something else. Dorian already has one." Juliette turned the box over. "My mom said I could put it on her credit card and pay her back from my allowance. Ten dollars a month. That's the smart way."

Thalia frowned. "Fifteen months of allowance for a headset you could buy in fifteen weeks of saving anyway. Where's the smart part?"

Juliette had no answer, so she ate her fries. That afternoon Mr. Suryanto's math class had bank day, where they ran the school's little savings counter in the gym, and Juliette had been named savings ambassador, mostly because she owned a blazer. A fourth grader came up with crumpled bills to deposit and asked, while Juliette wrote his balance in the ledger, why his father had paid the bank more money last month than he'd borrowed from it.

"Interest," said Dorian from the coin-counting station, not looking up. "Interest is the price of borrowing money. It gets charged as a percentage of what you borrowed."

"Like renting money," the fourth grader said, and Dorian shrugged, which was as close to enthusiasm as he got.

Juliette sat very still behind the counter. A percentage. Of what you borrowed. She took out her notebook and wrote the headset price, then ten dollars a month, and made herself do the multiplication all the way to the end, twice, because she wanted to verify it was wrong and it refused to be. Her mom's card charged interest every month the balance sat there, and Juliette's allowance payments were small, so the balance would sit there a long time. She would end up paying back more than two hundred forty dollars. For the same headset. The one already on sale.

At recess she found Dorian by the fence. "You wanted the Skyrider for months," she said. "How'd you get yours?"

"Birthday. Why?" He squinted at her. "Also, Thalia wants you to save with us for the class trip, but she was too polite to say it at lunch."

Juliette walked to the library, took out a fresh sheet, and wrote SAVE FIRST at the top, then crossed it out and wrote SAVE FIRST, THALIA'S TRIP TOO, which was longer but more honest. She taped it inside her locker, right where the headset ad had been.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Every morning something dug in the seedbed behind the garage, and every morning Kaitlyn counted fewer marigold seeds than she had planted the day before. She had seen no tracks, no fur, no slime, nothing but little craters in the soil. Her mother suggested birds. Ellen suggested squirrels. Kira suggested Kaitlyn count better, which was not helpful.

"You can't see what's doing it," Kaitlyn said, kneeling at the bed with a trowel. "So you make a guess and then you test it. Ms. Rossi calls it a hypothesis." She had written hers on an index card and tucked it under a flowerpot: birds are stealing the seeds. "If I'm right, a cage over the seeds stops it. If the seeds still vanish, I'm wrong, and it's something that crawls."

She set up two dishes in the garden, both on the ground, both in the same patch of sun, since the bees that pollinated the squash nearby seemed to like it warm and she figured seed thieves might too. Ten seeds in each dish, counted twice, because of Kira. She pressed the dishes into the soil at the same depth, so the temperature would be the same around both, and she would check them at the same time each morning. The only difference would be the cage: one dish covered with chicken wire, one open to the sky.

"It's just ten seeds," Ellen said, watching Kaitlyn clip the wire. "Seems trivial."

"It's not trivial if it's the whole test. If I put out different amounts, or check one dish at seven and one at noon, I'd never know whether it was the cage that mattered or something else. Everything except the thing I'm testing has to stay the same. Same amount, same temperature, same timing." She set the cage down over the first dish with a firm little click.

The first morning, both dishes were untouched, which annoyed her more than theft would have. The second morning, the open dish held six seeds and a small crater; the caged dish held ten, flat and undisturbed. The third morning, the open dish was empty, and when Kaitlyn leaned close she found a single grey feather stuck to the rim of the cage.

She pulled the index card out from under the flowerpot and added one word in careful capitals. Behind her, a mourning dove landed on the fence, looked at the chicken wire, and looked at her.

"All right," Kaitlyn said. "The wire stays."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The main grain crops of ancient Egypt were emmer wheat and barley, used to make the bread and beer that were everyday food for most people.
story:
The museum's Egypt wing smelled like dust and old stone, and Colton stood in front of a glass case holding two round loaves so dark and cracked they looked like rocks. Ms. Weiss had given each student a topic to present on the spot, and his was the Nile. He had practiced on the bus, but Bernard had just leaned over and whispered, "You said they grew corn. Corn came from the Americas, genius."

Colton felt his ears go hot. He revised his plan fast, the way he did when a math answer came out wrong and he had to find where the mistake started. Corn was out. But what was in? He stared at the loaves and the little plaque beside them, then at a long table behind the case where Lea was already turning a crank on a model of a canal. Water sloshed through a gate with a brass valve, and when she opened it, the water spread across a flat tray of green paper shaped like a river valley.

"Look," Lea said. "Flood comes, valve opens, water goes everywhere the farmers want it."

Colton joined her at the model. The flood soaked the tray, and when the water drained away, the green paper looked darker, like a field ready for planting. That was the pattern he needed. The river flooded, the water fed the fields, the fields grew the grain, and the grain fed everyone. It was not some sophisticated machine doing the work. It was the river itself, arriving every year without being asked.

When his turn came, Colton pointed at the loaves in the case. "They didn't grow corn," he said. "The main grain crops were emmer wheat and barley. That's what those loaves are made of. Barley went into their beer too, and bread and beer were everyday food for most people." He nodded at the flood model. "The Nile made it possible. And a whole kingdom of people, fed on grain, could build the pyramids."

Ms. Weiss wrote something on her clipboard. Bernard gave him a slow thumbs-up from the back.

"Nice save," Bernard said. "Emmer wheat. Who knew?"

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Aurora stood in line at the mall pretzel stand, holding her birthday money, trying to decide between the headphones she had wanted for a month and the sneakers everyone at school seemed to be wearing. Reese had gotten the sneakers first, and after that it was like a rule had spread through sixth grade: two more kids had them by Friday, and Edwin had put them on his birthday list without even trying them on. Aurora could still picture herself last month, begging her mom for a fidget toy because "everyone has one," and how that toy now sat at the bottom of her backpack collecting crumbs. She did not want to do that again with forty dollars.

While she waited, she scrolled her phone. A video popped up of a famous singer raving about the exact sneakers, calling them "revolutionary, legendary, the greatest thing ever made for your feet." Aurora's thumb hovered. The words felt warm and heavy, like the adjectives had been chosen to lift the shoes up and crush every other brand at the same time. Then she noticed the caption. At the very end, in small letters, was "#ad."

She tapped the profile of a second reviewer, a guy who tested shoes for fun. His video was calmer. "Here's the thing," he said to the camera, holding up a box. "In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something." No "#ad" anywhere on his page, and no free sneakers either, as far as she could tell. He actually showed where the stitching rubbed his ankle after a week.

Aurora had a simple test: if a review glowed too brightly, she would hunt for the disclosure before trusting it. She scrolled the singer's page again. There it was on three more posts, tiny as plumbing hidden inside a wall, doing its quiet work where nobody looked. The glowing words suddenly seemed less like facts and more like a paycheck.

The pretzel line moved. Aurora stepped up, ordered a cinnamon twist, and texted Edwin, who was leaning against a pillar near the fountain, waiting. He wandered over, phone out, perpendicular to the pillar like he was too cool to actually lean on it. "Did you see the singer's video?" he asked. "Those sneakers are legendary."

"Legendary and paid for," Aurora said, holding up her screen. "See the hashtag? She got them free."

fact: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, the same substance as a gas, so boiling is a physical change even though it makes bubbles.
story:
Adam had taped a sign above his project that read "BUBBLES MEAN A CHEMICAL CHANGE," and for the first twenty minutes of the science fair, nobody argued with him. Kyson stopped by, looked at his chart of vinegar and baking soda, and nodded. "The bubbles are the proof," Kyson said. "New stuff got made."

Then Aliya leaned over the table next to Adam's, where her project sat. She had a hot plate, a beaker of water, and a thermometer. "So what's happening in mine?" she asked. The water had gone turbulent, rolling and churning, and bubbles climbed its sides in a steady stream.

"Chemical change," Adam said. "Bubbles. Same as mine."

"Watch the side of the beaker," Aliya said. "See the bubbles form down there, where the heat is." She tapped the glass. "If something new was being made, where would it go after the bubbles pop?"

Adam crouched so his eyes were level with the rim. A bubble reached the surface, opened, and a puff of white drifted up and vanished. He watched another one do the same thing. In his vinegar demonstration, the bubbles had come from the liquid and the powder making something different together. Here there was only water and heat. He straightened up.

"It's steam," he said. "The bubbles are water vapour, the same stuff as a gas. Nothing new gets made." He pulled the marker off the table and crossed out his sign, then wrote underneath, "BOILING IS A PHYSICAL CHANGE." He said it again, quieter, checking it against the beaker. "Still water. Just gas now."

Ms. Abdi came by on her judging rounds and read both lines, the crossed-out one and the new one. "Which one do you emphasize, then, if someone asks you today?" she asked.

"The second one," Adam said. "The first one's how I got here."

Aliya ladled out a spoonful of the boiled water and held it up so the judges could see it was clear, still water, and Adam pointed at the line on his sign.
